chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Mechanics of Competitive Devaluation

lessons.title: RBI Intervention and India's Forex Reserves: The Defense Playbook

body.text: The RBI's playbook is not about pushing the rupee down for advantage. It is about defending against disorderly moves in both directions, using every tool from the previous lesson, spot intervention, forward swaps, rate policy and jawboning, deliberately without ever announcing a target level.

children.text: The RBI's Version of the Four Tools

The RBI has access to the same four tools from the last lesson, deployed with an important difference: it uses them defensively, on both sides of the market, and almost never announces a specific level it is defending. It buys dollars to slow excessive rupee strength and sells dollars to slow excessive weakness, using public sector banks such as SBI as its operational arm in the interbank market so its own trades don't always announce themselves.

markDefs.definition: The number of months of a country's imports that its foreign exchange reserves could cover if all other capital inflows stopped, a standard measure of reserve adequacy that the RBI and IMF both track.

children.text: How much room the RBI has to defend the rupee at any given moment comes down largely to its reserves relative to
, the crisis-era metric that fell to barely a few weeks in 1991, covered in Chapter 1. The RBI has spent every year since building that buffer specifically so it never faces that constraint again.
Case Study: The 2013 Taper Tantrum Defense

In May 2013, then Fed Chair Ben Bernanke signalled the Fed might start tapering its bond purchases. The carry trade capital that had flooded emerging markets during the QE era covered in Chapter 1 reversed hard and fast. India, running a large current account deficit at the time, was one of the hardest hit: the rupee fell from around ₹54 to the dollar in May 2013 to a record intraday low near ₹68.85 by late August, a collapse that put the RBI's entire defense toolkit to work simultaneously.

body.title: Size the 2013 Fall
body.prompt: The rupee fell from approximately ₹54 to the dollar in May 2013 to a record low of approximately ₹68.85 by late August 2013. Approximately what percentage did the rupee depreciate over this period? Round to the nearest whole percent.
body.explanation: (68.85 − 54) / 54 = 14.85 / 54 ≈ 27.5%, roughly a 27 to 28% fall in under four months, among the sharpest moves the rupee has seen since the managed float began in 1993.

body.title: The RBI's 2013 Defense, Tool by Tool

events.title: Bernanke's taper remarks
events.description: The Fed signals a possible start to tapering QE3 bond purchases, triggering a broad emerging market sell-off that hits the rupee hard.

events.title: RBI tightens liquidity sharply
events.description: The RBI raises the Marginal Standing Facility rate by 200 basis points to 10.25% and caps banks' access to cheaper liquidity windows, an emergency move to make rupee speculation more expensive, ahead of any swap scheme.

events.title: Rupee hits a record low
events.description: The rupee touches an intraday low near ₹68.85 to the dollar, its weakest level on record at the time.

events.title: Raghuram Rajan takes charge, launches the FCNR(B) swap scheme
events.description: On his first day as Governor, Rajan announces a special swap window offering banks a concessional, fixed swap cost of 3.5% a year to raise fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits from NRIs, well below prevailing market swap rates.

events.title: Roughly $34 billion raised
events.description: Banks raise approximately $34 billion in fresh FCNR(B) deposits through the scheme, giving the RBI a large, low-cost inflow of dollars without directly touching its own spot reserves.

events.title: Rupee stabilises
events.description: The rupee recovers to around ₹61 to ₹62 to the dollar as confidence returns, and the RBI begins unwinding the emergency liquidity tightening from July.

body.caption: Every Tool From Lesson 1, Deployed in 2013

cells: MSF rate hiked 200bps to 10.25% in July 2013
Made short rupee positions costlier to fund, discouraging speculative selling
FCNR(B) swap window at a concessional 3.5% cost
Raised roughly $34 billion in fresh dollar inflows without depleting spot reserves
Rajan's early, confident public communication on reserves and reform
Rebuilt market confidence independent of any single transaction

body.title: Quick Check: Why a Swap Scheme, Not Just Spot Selling?
body.question: Why did the RBI design a special FCNR(B) swap scheme in 2013 rather than simply selling more dollars from its existing reserves to defend the rupee?
options: Because spot intervention was illegal under Indian law at the time
Because the swap scheme brought in fresh dollar inflows at a controlled cost, defending the rupee without running down the RBI's own existing reserve buffer
Because FCNR deposits are denominated in rupees, not dollars
Because the scheme was purely symbolic and had no real effect on the rupee
body.explanation: Selling from existing reserves defends the rupee but depletes the buffer built specifically to avoid another 1991. The FCNR(B) swap scheme instead attracted new dollar inflows from NRIs at a fixed, below-market cost to banks, adding to reserves indirectly rather than spending them down, which is precisely why it is remembered as one of the RBI's most creative defense tools.

children.text: The Other Direction: Sterilising Inflows, Not Just Defending Against Outflows

markDefs.definition: A facility that lets the RBI issue government-backed bonds specifically to absorb the domestic rupee liquidity created when it buys dollars in the forex market, keeping large forex purchases from fuelling excess money supply growth.

children.text: The 2013 episode shows the RBI defending against weakness, but roughly half of its job is the opposite: capping excessive rupee strength during heavy capital inflow periods, such as the QE-driven wave of 2009 to 2011 covered in Chapter 1, or the extraordinary global liquidity flood of 2020 to 2021 during the pandemic, when India's reserves climbed to record highs near $642 billion by September 2021. Buying dollars to prevent the rupee from appreciating too fast injects rupee liquidity into the banking system, which the RBI then absorbs through the
or variable rate reverse repo operations, so the intervention doesn't spill over into unwanted inflation.

body.title: Defending Against Weakness vs Defending Against Strength

columns.label: Rupee too weak (2013-style)
points: RBI sells dollars from reserves, or arranges fresh inflows via swap schemes
May pair this with a rate hike to discourage speculative selling
Relies heavily on jawboning and confidence-building to stop a self-reinforcing slide
Constrained by how large the reserve buffer actually is

columns.label: Rupee too strong (2009-11, 2020-21 style)
points: RBI buys dollars, adding to reserves rather than spending them
Sterilises the resulting rupee liquidity via MSS bonds or reverse repo operations
Less urgent politically, since exporters complain but there's no default-risk pressure
Constrained mainly by the cost and complexity of sterilisation, not by running out of ammunition

body.text: Compare this to the SNB's franc floor from the last lesson. The SNB announced an explicit level, 1.20 francs per euro, and defended it publicly for over three years before abandoning it overnight. The RBI deliberately does the opposite: it never confirms a target level, which keeps speculators guessing about exactly where it will show up and denies them a clean, one-way bet. The cost of this opacity is that markets sometimes misjudge the RBI's tolerance; the benefit is that the RBI is never trapped defending a specific number the way the SNB eventually was.

body.title: You Are on the RBI's Currency Desk
body.scenario: The rupee has fallen 6% against the dollar over three weeks amid a broad emerging-market sell-off following an unexpected US rate move. Reserves are healthy at roughly 10 months of import cover, well above 1991-era levels, but exporters and importers alike are asking for clarity on where things stabilise, and speculative short positions on the rupee are building on the NSE's currency derivatives segment.
body.prompt: Do you announce a defended level the way the SNB once did for the franc, or hold to the RBI's traditional no-target approach? Justify your choice.
body.modelAnswer: Hold to the no-target approach. Announcing a specific defended level, as the SNB did at 1.20 francs per euro, hands speculators a single, clear line to test, and if reserves or political tolerance ever fall short of what's needed to defend it, the eventual abandonment (as with the January 2015 Swiss franc shock) is far more disruptive than a gradual, undefined slide would have been. With 10 months of import cover, the RBI has real room to intervene selectively on the sharpest days, use jawboning to signal it is watching closely without commiting to a number, and reserve larger tools like a swap scheme for if the move becomes disorderly rather than merely uncomfortable. Clarity for exporters and importers is better delivered through steady central bank communication about intent and available tools, not through a target that becomes a target for speculators too.

cards.definition: The number of months of imports a country's forex reserves could fund if all other inflows stopped, a key reserve adequacy metric.
A special RBI window offering banks a concessional swap cost to raise fresh FCNR(B) dollar deposits, raising roughly $34 billion during the 2013 taper tantrum.
A facility letting the RBI issue bonds to absorb the rupee liquidity created by its dollar purchases, sterilising forex intervention.
The RBI's practice of intervening to limit both excessive rupee weakness and excessive rupee strength, unlike a one-directional peg defense.

points: The RBI uses the same four tools from Lesson 1, rate policy, spot intervention, swap markets and jawboning, but deploys them defensively in both directions and without announcing a target level.
The 2013 taper tantrum, triggered by Bernanke's QE tapering remarks, sent the rupee down roughly 27 to 28% from May to August 2013, prompting a coordinated multi-tool RBI response.
The FCNR(B) swap scheme launched by Raghuram Rajan in September 2013 raised roughly $34 billion in fresh dollar inflows at a controlled cost, defending the rupee without depleting existing reserves.
The RBI also intervenes to cap excessive rupee strength during heavy inflow periods, sterilising the resulting liquidity through the Market Stabilisation Scheme or reverse repo operations.
Unlike the SNB's explicit franc floor, the RBI deliberately avoids confirming a defended level, trading some clarity for the flexibility to never be trapped defending a specific number.
Import cover, not political preference, is usually the real constraint on how aggressively the RBI can defend the rupee at any given moment.
